hints: Notice the axes: $E_K$ is plotted against height $h$ above the ground, so the right side of the graph is high up and the origin $h=0$ is the ground.
Think about energy at the two ends: $E_K=0$ when released from rest at maximum $h$, and $E_K$ is maximum when $h=0$ just before impact.
Use $mgh + E_K = \text{constant}$ with no air resistance to show $E_K = \text{constant} - mgh$, which is a straight line with negative gradient.
walkthrough: Identify the start and end: released from rest means $E_K = 0$ at the maximum $h$, and falling means $E_K$ is maximum at $h = 0$.
State conservation of mechanical energy with negligible air resistance: gravitational potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy gained.
Write total energy at release height $H$ as $mgH$, so at any lower height $h$: $mgh + E_K = mgH$.
Rearrange to $E_K = mgH - mgh$, which is of the form $y = c - mx$ with $y = E_K$ and $x = h$.
Interpret this as a straight line of gradient $-mg$ that intercepts the $E_K$-axis at $mgH$ and the $h$-axis at $H$.
Only the straight line that falls to zero as $h$ increases matches this. This is option D.

options.A: Incorrect. This shows $E_K$ increasing with $h$ with a curve, but $E_K$ must be largest when $h=0$ at the ground.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows $E_K$ increasing linearly with $h$, but a falling ball gains kinetic energy as height decreases.
options.C: Incorrect. This has the correct trend of $E_K$ decreasing with $h$, but the variation is curved whereas $E_K$ is linear in $h$.
options.D: Correct. $E_K$ decreases linearly to zero as $h$ increases to the release height, matching conservation of energy.
